heuristics.rule: Apply tech recruiting logic only to tech; each industry has a different sponsorship and recruiting structure
heuristics.condition: When an international student is job searching in finance, consulting, biotech, or policy...
heuristics.action: ...use industry-specific sponsorship data, recruiting calendars, and target employer lists rather than generic international student advice
heuristics.because: Most international student job search advice is implicitly written for tech, producing systematically wrong guidance when applied to other industries

heuristics.rule: Target bulge-bracket banks and large asset managers for finance sponsorship; avoid boutiques unless verified
heuristics.condition: When an international student is pursuing investment banking or asset management...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Citi, BofA, Barclays, Deutsche Bank and large asset managers over middle-market or boutique firms
heuristics.because: Middle-market banks sponsor inconsistently and boutique investment banks (10–30 people) often do not sponsor at all

heuristics.rule: Verify sponsorship via USCIS data before investing significant time in any smaller or unknown employer
heuristics.condition: When the employer is not a well-known large company in any sector...
heuristics.action: ...look up their H-1B petition history in USCIS data before applying or pursuing their process
heuristics.because: Smaller firms rarely disclose sponsorship limitations upfront, and investing time in a non-sponsor wastes OPT runway

heuristics.rule: For finance recruiting, network to uncover sponsorship policies before applying because the information is opaque
heuristics.condition: When targeting finance firms where sponsorship status is unclear...
heuristics.action: ...network into contacts at those firms to learn their sponsorship policy before committing to the application process
heuristics.because: Finance recruiting is much more opaque than tech, with less public information about which firms sponsor

heuristics.rule: Treat the internship-to-return-offer path as the primary strategy in tech and MBB consulting
heuristics.condition: When targeting large tech companies or MBB consulting firms...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize securing an internship over directly applying for full-time roles
heuristics.because: The internship → return offer path works best in these industries, with MBB return offer rates at 70–85% for summer associates

heuristics.rule: Use cap-exempt employment as a bridge after multiple H-1B lottery losses
heuristics.condition: When an international student has lost the H-1B lottery multiple years in a row...
heuristics.action: ...pursue employment at universities, research nonprofits, or affiliated research institutions that are cap-exempt
heuristics.because: Cap-exempt employers can file H-1B petitions at any time without lottery, eliminating the annual lottery risk

heuristics.rule: For tech startups, treat companies under 50 people as high-risk for sponsorship regardless of verbal assurances
heuristics.condition: When a small tech startup says they will 'figure out sponsorship'...
heuristics.action: ...treat this as a red flag and verify whether they have ever successfully sponsored an H-1B before accepting an offer
heuristics.because: Tech startups under 50 people rarely have immigration infrastructure, and a CTO who has never done it before creates execution risk

heuristics.rule: For life sciences PhDs, prioritize large pharma and established biotech for maximum sponsorship reliability
heuristics.condition: When a PhD graduate in biology, chemistry, or pharmacology is job searching...
heuristics.action: ...target Pfizer, Moderna, Genentech, Merck, J&J, BMS and other large established companies first
heuristics.because: Large pharma sponsors reliably while CROs and smaller biotechs are variable, and the STEM OPT + large pharma combination is one of the most reliable pathways in life sciences

heuristics.rule: Missing fall recruiting is nearly catastrophic for MBB consulting via on-campus routes
heuristics.condition: When targeting McKinsey, BCG, or Bain through campus recruiting...
heuristics.action: ...prioritize fall recruiting (September–November) as the primary application window, treating it as non-negotiable
heuristics.because: MBB recruiting is heavily structured around fall campus cycles, and missing it forecloses the primary access route

heuristics.rule: Geographic flexibility significantly expands employer pool in biotech
heuristics.condition: When a life sciences candidate is restricting their job search geographically...
heuristics.action: ...expand willingness to work in San Francisco Bay Area, Boston/Cambridge, San Diego, or Research Triangle (NC)
heuristics.because: Biotech sponsoring employers are geographically concentrated in these clusters, and geographic restriction artificially narrows an already concentrated market

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Sponsorship rates differ dramatically by industry — applying the same strategy across industries produces wrong outcomes
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Cross-reference USCIS H-1B petition data for specific employers in the target industry; consult the industry comparison matrix

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Even in sponsorship-friendly industries, small companies (under 50 people in tech, boutiques in finance/consulting) often cannot or do not sponsor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check USCIS historical petition data; ask directly whether the company has previously sponsored H-1B and who handled immigration

decision_factors.factor: STEM OPT eligibility of the degree
decision_factors.why_it_matters: STEM OPT extends work authorization to 3 years, dramatically changing the risk profile for employers and providing more time before H-1B dependency
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check whether the degree program is on the DHS STEM OPT designated degree program list; finance degrees are less often STEM-designated than CS or engineering

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Each industry has a different recruiting calendar; applying at the wrong time makes candidates structurally invisible
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Map target industry recruiting windows: finance is August–November (earliest), consulting is September–November, tech is year-round with fall/spring peaks

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Cap-exempt employers eliminate H-1B lottery risk entirely, which is the single largest source of employment uncertainty for international students
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine if employer is a university, affiliated research institution, or nonprofit with primary research/educational purpose

decision_factors.factor: H-1B petition complexity by role type
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Some roles (e.g., finance) face higher RFE/denial rates because the specialty occupation requirement is more contested, creating additional risk even at sponsoring firms
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research whether the role type has historically faced specialty occupation challenges; finance roles are more contested than software engineering roles

decision_factors.why_it_matters: In concentrated industries like biotech, geographic flexibility directly expands the available pool of sponsoring employers
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify geographic hubs for the target industry; assess whether candidate is willing to relocate to those hubs

decision_factors.factor: Degree level relative to industry norms
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Sponsorship access differs significantly by degree level in some industries — biotech is excellent for PhDs but limited for undergrads
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Research typical credential requirements at target employers; understand whether the role being targeted typically requires a specific degree level

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Cap-exempt employers pay 20–40% less than private sector equivalents — candidates must decide whether immigration certainty is worth the pay cut
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare compensation ranges at cap-exempt vs. cap-subject employers in the same field; calculate total expected value given lottery odds

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Pursuing boutique investment banks or consulting firms instead of large firms
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Many boutiques do not sponsor and will not tell you upfront, consuming significant recruiting time before the issue surfaces
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Finance and consulting international students who optimize for prestige of boutique brand without verifying sponsorship first

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a cap-exempt employer (university, research nonprofit) for immigration stability
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Compensation is 20–40% lower than private sector equivalents, compounding over years if the role becomes long-term
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who use cap-exempt employment as a bridge but stay longer than planned due to inertia or green card processing timelines

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a role at a tech startup under 50 people based on a verbal promise to 'figure out sponsorship'
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The company may lack immigration infrastructure, causing the H-1B petition to be filed incorrectly, delayed, or abandoned under cost pressure
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students prioritizing role quality or startup equity over immigration certainty

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Targeting finance roles at large banks for sponsorship reliability
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Finance H-1B petitions face higher specialty occupation scrutiny, meaning even well-resourced sponsors carry more petition risk than equivalent tech roles
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who assume large bank = automatic H-1B approval analogous to large tech company

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Restricting job search geography in biotech/life sciences
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The pool of sponsoring biotech employers is heavily concentrated in four geographic clusters, so geographic restriction dramatically shrinks the realistic employer target list
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Life sciences candidates with geographic constraints due to family, relationships, or cost of living preferences

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Waiting until offer stage to disclose visa status in finance
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Finance firms sometimes screen out international candidates during initial screens — early disclosure can save time even if it costs some opportunities
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students applying a tech-optimized disclosure strategy (wait until offer) to finance recruiting without understanding the sector difference

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying tech job search advice wholesale to non-tech industries
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Most available international student job search resources are implicitly written for tech; candidates assume the advice generalizes
failure_patterns.consequence: Wrong recruiting calendar, wrong disclosure timing, wrong employer targeting — systematic misalignment with how non-tech industries actually hire
warning_signs: Using year-round rolling application strategy for finance or MBB consulting
Targeting tech-style networking (LinkedIn cold outreach) as primary strategy for finance where in-person relationships dominate

failure_patterns.pattern: Investing significant time in boutique finance or consulting firms without verifying sponsorship first
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Boutique firms are prestigious and attractive, and they don't proactively disclose sponsorship limitations; candidates assume prestige correlates with sponsorship
failure_patterns.consequence: Wasted OPT runway and recruiting cycles on firms that will ultimately decline to sponsor
warning_signs: No USCIS petition history found for the firm
Firm has fewer than 30 employees and no dedicated HR or legal infrastructure

failure_patterns.pattern: Missing fall recruiting windows for finance and consulting by treating them like tech rolling applications
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates don't realize how early and structured finance and consulting recruiting is, especially for internships
failure_patterns.consequence: Structural exclusion from the primary internship pipeline for that year, with limited remediation options
warning_signs: Starting finance or consulting job search in January or February expecting the same access as October
Not attending fall campus recruiting events at the start of the academic year

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming large company = automatic sponsorship in all industries
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Large tech companies do sponsor aggressively and predictably, so candidates extrapolate this to large companies in other sectors
failure_patterns.consequence: Pursuing companies that are large but inconsistent sponsors (middle-market banks, Tier 2 consulting boutiques) without verification
warning_signs: Not checking USCIS petition data for firms outside of FAANG-equivalent
Relying only on Glassdoor or word-of-mouth rather than actual petition records

failure_patterns.pattern: Undergrads in life sciences targeting roles without accounting for degree-level sponsorship differences
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Biotech's reputation as sponsorship-friendly is built primarily on PhD-level hiring; undergrads assume the same conditions apply
failure_patterns.consequence: Frustration and failed applications at biotech firms that sponsor PhDs but not undergrad research associates
warning_signs: Targeting biotech companies known primarily as PhD employers without identifying undergrad-specific hiring programs
CROs or small biotechs appearing in the target list without sponsorship verification

diagnostic_questions.question: Which industry are you targeting, and are you using advice specific to that industry or general international student advice?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate's strategy is calibrated to the actual sponsorship and recruiting dynamics of their target industry
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the recruiting calendar for that industry, and have you mapped your application timeline against it?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You may be applying tech-optimized advice to a non-tech context — revalidate your targeting, disclosure timing, and recruiting calendar

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you verified sponsorship for each target employer using USCIS petition data, not just reputation or verbal assurances?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate's employer list is based on actual evidence or assumptions — reputation and size do not reliably predict sponsorship in non-tech industries
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What did the petition history show, and did you filter out firms with no prior H-1B filings?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Significant risk of investing time in non-sponsors, especially in finance boutiques and smaller consulting firms

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your degree program STEM-designated for OPT purposes?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate has 1 year or 3 years of OPT, which fundamentally changes the timeline and risk exposure before H-1B dependency
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are you targeting employers who are familiar with STEM OPT extensions and willing to wait through the OPT window before H-1B filing?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: With only 1 year of OPT, your lottery exposure is immediate — prioritize large verified sponsors and consider cap-exempt employment as a contingency

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you lost the H-1B lottery, and if so, how many times?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate needs to consider alternative immigration pathways, including cap-exempt employment
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you identified cap-exempt employers (universities, research nonprofits) in your field as a bridge option?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Continue primary strategy but build cap-exempt contingency into the plan from the start

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you geographically flexible, and does your target industry have geographic concentration?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether geographic constraints are artificially limiting the available pool of sponsoring employers, especially in biotech
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you prioritized the key geographic clusters for your industry in your job search?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Understand that geographic restriction in a concentrated industry (like biotech) dramatically reduces your viable employer pool

diagnostic_questions.question: For finance or consulting: are you targeting bulge-bracket or MBB-tier firms, or are you targeting boutiques?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the candidate's target list is concentrated in reliable sponsors or distributed across firms with inconsistent or no sponsorship
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Good — but have you verified each firm individually rather than assuming tier equals sponsorship?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Boutique finance and consulting firms frequently do not sponsor; verify each one before investing recruiting effort

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your degree level — undergrad, master's, or PhD — and does it match the typical hiring profile at your target employers?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether there is a mismatch between candidate credentials and the degree level at which the target employer typically sponsors
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are you targeting roles with a realistic conversion to H-1B, or roles where sponsorship is inconsistent at your degree level?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Recalibrate target employer list to firms that sponsor at your degree level — especially critical in biotech where PhD vs. undergrad sponsorship rates diverge significantly

industry_realities.common_belief: Visa sponsorship advice applies uniformly across industries
industry_realities.actual_reality: Sponsorship landscape, recruiting calendar, and strategy differ significantly by industry; tech advice applied to finance or consulting produces systematically wrong guidance
industry_realities.implication: International students must research industry-specific sponsorship dynamics rather than applying generic advice

industry_realities.common_belief: Large, well-known companies in any industry reliably sponsor H-1B
industry_realities.actual_reality: Sponsorship reliability is excellent in tech and large pharma, good but not automatic at bulge-bracket banks, and inconsistent at mid-tier firms in finance and consulting
industry_realities.implication: Company size and brand recognition are insufficient proxies for sponsorship reliability outside of tech; USCIS data verification is required

industry_realities.common_belief: Boutique investment banks and consulting firms that are prestigious and well-known will sponsor international students
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many boutique finance and consulting firms (10–30 people) do not sponsor at all and will not proactively disclose this
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should verify sponsorship status before investing recruiting time in boutique firms, not after receiving an offer or late in the process

industry_realities.common_belief: Finance H-1B sponsorship works the same as tech H-1B sponsorship at large employers
industry_realities.actual_reality: Finance H-1B petitions face higher specialty occupation scrutiny and are more work for immigration counsel, creating additional risk even at large, experienced sponsors
industry_realities.implication: Finance candidates should factor in petition complexity and potential RFE risk even when targeting top-tier banks that sponsor

industry_realities.common_belief: The biotech/pharma industry is uniformly good for international student sponsorship
industry_realities.actual_reality: Biotech sponsorship is excellent for STEM PhDs at large companies, but is limited and variable for undergrads, and CROs and small biotechs are inconsistent sponsors regardless of degree level
industry_realities.implication: Life sciences candidates must assess sponsorship relative to their specific degree level and target company size, not the industry's aggregate reputation

industry_realities.common_belief: Working for the US government or government contractors is a viable option for international students
industry_realities.actual_reality: US federal employment requires citizenship or permanent residence in most agencies; government contractor roles often require security clearances that are unavailable to F-1/H-1B holders
industry_realities.implication: International students should effectively exclude direct federal government and most government contractor roles from their target list unless specifically verified

industry_realities.common_belief: Cap-exempt employers are a niche fallback option for unusual circumstances
industry_realities.actual_reality: For international students who lose the H-1B lottery multiple years in a row, cap-exempt employment (universities, research nonprofits) is the primary structural solution — not a niche fallback
industry_realities.implication: Cap-exempt employer targets should be built into every international student's job search strategy from the start as a planned contingency

industry_realities.common_belief: Finance and consulting recruiting timelines are similar to tech — you can apply throughout the year
industry_realities.actual_reality: Finance recruiting is the earliest of any major industry, with internship processes starting in August–October for the following summer; missing this window closes the primary pipeline
industry_realities.implication: International students targeting finance or MBB consulting must start recruiting preparation earlier than any other industry — fall of the academic year is the primary window, not spring

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes large or prestigious companies sponsor based on reputation, word of mouth, or Glassdoor reviews
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Verifies sponsorship for each target employer using USCIS H-1B petition data before investing recruiting time
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Boutique firms and mid-tier companies frequently do not sponsor; reputation-based assumptions waste OPT runway on non-sponsors

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Applies a single job search strategy across all industries, often derived from tech-focused international student advice
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Builds industry-specific strategies for recruiting calendar, disclosure timing, employer targeting, and petition risk
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Using tech recruiting logic for finance or consulting produces structural misalignment with how those industries actually hire

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Starts finance or consulting applications in January or spring, treating it like rolling tech recruiting
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Starts finance and consulting recruiting preparation in August–September, treating the fall window as the primary and non-negotiable application period
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Missing fall recruiting for finance or MBB consulting structurally excludes candidates from the primary pipeline for that cycle

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses entirely on the primary target industry and employer list without building a cap-exempt contingency
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Identifies cap-exempt employer options from the start and treats them as a planned secondary pathway, not a last resort
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: H-1B lottery failure is a real probabilistic outcome; not having a cap-exempt contingency means lottery loss becomes a crisis rather than a managed transition

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Accepts verbal assurances from startup leadership ('we'll figure out the sponsorship') as sufficient due diligence
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Asks specifically whether the company has previously sponsored H-1B, who handled immigration, and whether they have external immigration counsel engaged
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Startups without immigration infrastructure can fail to execute on sponsorship commitments, leaving the candidate without status

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Assumes that an industry's general sponsorship reputation applies uniformly regardless of degree level
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Assesses sponsorship likelihood at the specific intersection of degree level and company type — e.g., recognizing that biotech sponsorship for undergrads is fundamentally different from biotech sponsorship for PhDs
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Targeting employers who sponsor at a different degree level than the candidate's credential produces mismatch and rejection without explanation

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Applies a uniform disclosure timing rule (e.g., 'always wait until offer') derived from tech advice across all industries
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Calibrates disclosure timing by industry — waiting in tech where OPT is normalized, but researching and disclosing earlier in finance where some firms screen out early
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Wrong disclosure timing in finance can waste multiple rounds of interviews on firms that would have screened out earlier — or cause premature rejection in tech by disclosing too early
